title: Screen Time That Keeps Caribbean Culture Close
excerpt: The screen is already in the house. The useful question is what is on it, who presses play, and whether the child still hears the islands.
content:
Most families are not choosing between a screen and a perfect afternoon outside. They are choosing what the screen is for after school, in the car, or while dinner is on the stove. Caribbean culture can be part of that choice without pretending a tablet raises the child.

Parents stay in charge

You pick the time. You sit close when you can. You turn it off. Likkle Legends does not sell anything to children inside the portal. There is no kid checkout and no toy-shop button in the child's view. If a paid Island Pack or annual plan is used, a parent completes checkout, and access starts only after payment is verified.

Free Forever is a rotating library plus the kid-safe portal, not a promise of every story on day one. Details are in free Caribbean learning for ages 3–9.

A simple screen pattern for ages 3–9

  • Start with a song on Likkle Radio. Listening is free and needs no account.
  • Read or play one story together. Ask what the character wanted, not whether the child "got it right."
  • If there is still energy, play one game. Public options include Island Hop (flags and capitals with Mango Moko), Tanty's Kitchen (sorting ingredients for Caribbean dishes), and R.O.T.I.'s Math Market (counting and change).
  • Inside a parent account, portal games include Caribbean Flag Match, Island Trivia Quest, and Island Memory Match.
  • Stop while the child still likes it. Ending on a win makes the next day easier.

When the day is already loud

Island Helpers sit beside stories. Calm Mode softens motion and surprise sound. Phrase cards let a child tap a full line and hear it. First → Then is a simple picture plan, such as first a story, then a snack. Journey Stories are short books a parent writes or generates, then edits and publishes before a child can see them.

These are play supports. They are not a clinic, not a diagnosis, and not a medical device. If your child needs a specialist, use a specialist. Skip any tool that does not fit your family.

Culture is the point of the screen, not a sticker on it

A Caribbean game still counts as screen time. What it can do is keep flags, foods, and island names in the mix so the screen is not only somewhere else. Pair it with something off-screen: the real fruit, the real flag, or a call to family. That pairing is the lesson.

More on belonging away from the islands: teaching island pride in the diaspora.

faq.question: Is there a kid store or in-app purchase?
faq.answer: No. Children do not buy anything in the portal. Parents check out if they choose a paid plan. Access turns on only after that payment is verified.

faq.question: What can we do on a screen without an account?
faq.answer: Likkle Radio is free with no account. Public games such as Island Hop, Tanty's Kitchen, and R.O.T.I.'s Math Market are on the games page.

faq.question: Are Island Helpers a therapy tool?
faq.answer: No. Island Helpers are educational play supports. They are not a medical device, not therapy, and not a replacement for a speech-language pathologist or other specialist.
